note:
In this section, the Chronicler establishes the election and arrangement of the people of God from the beginning of history until the return of Judah from the Babylonian exile of the sixth century B.C. This election is the basis of the privileges and responsibilities of the readers as the continuing people of God.

Genealogies in the ancient Near East had a variety of forms and functions. Some of the passages in Chronicles trace a single family line through many generations (2:34–41). Others sketch several family lines together (6:1–3). The genealogies sometimes skip generations without notice, emphasizing significant persons and events (6:4–15). Ancient genealogies often included brief narratives highlighting important events, and the writer of Chronicles pauses on occasion to tell a story (4:9,10; 5:18–22).

Ancient genealogies set out not only family relations, but political, geographical, and social connections. Chronicles contains an assortment of lists, including families (e.g., 3:17–24), political relations (e.g., 2:24, 42, 45, 49–52), and trade guilds (e.g., 4:14, 21–23).

An essential purpose of the extensive genealogies in Chronicles is to convince the returned exiles of their true status as the legitimate continuation of God’s elect people. The writer works this out by reporting the election of Israel from all peoples (1:2–2:2), the arrangement of the tribes of Israel (2:3–9:1), and the representation of the tribes that returned from Babylon (9:16–34).

The genealogies focus on the order of the tribes of Israel, especially the role of the families of David and Levi. To receive the blessings of God, the people must observe carefully the divinely ordained arrangements. Their responsibility for obeying is established by their designation as God’s elect people.

Beginning with Noah, the account shows how God chose some nations over others. The sons of Noah are treated separately: Japheth (1:5–7), Ham (1:8–16), and Shem (1:17–27). Relying selectively on Gen. 10:1–32 (Gen. 10 note), the Chronicler places the chosen line last. From the descendants of Noah, the Shemites (Semitic peoples) alone were in special covenant relationship with God.

In ancient Near Eastern genealogies, the terms “sons” and “fathers” are often used literally. But they may be used more loosely, referring to relatively distant family relations or other social or geographical connections. Here “sons” points to cultural and geographical relationships. Cf. the geographical focus of 2:42–55; 4:1–23; 6:54–81; 7:20–29; 9:2; 11:10–47.

More attention is given to the Hamites than the Japhethites because Israel had more dealings with them. The list begins with all four sons of Ham but records only the descendants of Cush, Egypt, and Canaan. As a geographical term, “Cush” is the Hebrew for the area south of Egypt, modern-day northern Sudan. Though traditionally rendered “Ethiopia,” it did not stretch as far south as the modern country of that name.
Divine election narrows within the Shemites to Abraham’s family. The writer follows Gen. 10:21–31 closely and adds a brief summary of Gen. 11:10–27 to extend the genealogy to Abraham.
The plan of sovereign election is shown in the descendants of Abraham. As before, the writer deals first with those not chosen (1:29–33) and then with the chosen line in Isaac (1:34–2:2).

Following Genesis, the account distinguishes Ishmael’s descendants from the covenant line and deals with them before returning to the main focus.

**Ishmael.** He was promised great blessings from God (Gen. 16:11, 12), but he was not the heir of the covenant of grace God made with Abraham (Gen. 17:18–21).
See note on Gen. 25:1–4. Abraham’s descendants through Keturah were not from the line of promise in Isaac.
Esau and Jacob. See Gen. 25:27–34; 27:1–40.
This list follows Gen. 35:23–26 except for the position of Dan.

The writer has presented the twelve tribes of Israel as the goal of divine election. Now he describes the extent and order of the covenant nation, covering prominent figures in all the tribes except Dan and Zebulun. The lists involve not only people but also tribal territories. This is suggestive of a hope that the community of those returned from exile would eventually grow to include all the tribes and their territories (1:5 note). The tribes are presented in a symmetrical fashion, with the royal tribes of Judah (2:3–4:23) and Benjamin (8:1–40) at the start and finish and the priestly tribe of Levi at the center. The other tribes of lesser significance in the Chronicler’s history lesson are grouped between these tribes (see Outline of 1 Chronicles).

**2:3–4:23** Judah is placed first, a departure from the order of names announced in 2:1, 2. The priority of Judah reflects the importance of the throne of David for the hope of the returned exiles.

**2:3–9 sons of Judah.** These were Er, Onan, Shelah (by a Canaanite woman; Gen. 38:2), Perez, and Zerah (by Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law; Gen. 38:11–30). Perez and Hezron were ancestors of David.
Traditional wise men, compared with Solomon in 1 Kin. 4:31. Ethan and Heman probably should be distinguished from David’s musicians having the same names (15:19 and Pss. 88; 89).

A son of Zimri, who is mentioned in 2:6 (Josh. 7:1).

**broke faith.** Or, “acted unfaithfully.” This verb and the associated noun are a key part of the Chronicler’s theological vocabulary, denoting a willful abandonment of the terms of the covenant, often evidenced by failure to worship the LORD as He desired.

Departing from the order of Hezron’s sons presented in 2:9, Ram is placed first, as part of the line of David (2:3–4:23 note). This genealogical information is probably from the book of Ruth (Ruth 4:18–22).
According to 1 Sam. 17:12–14, David was Jesse’s eighth son. Elihu, another of Jesse’s sons, is mentioned in 1 Chr. 27:18 but omitted here, possibly because he had no children.
This Caleb is not “Caleb the son of Jephunneh” (Num. 13:6; 1 Chr. 4:15), but “Chelubai” (v. 9).

The line of Ram (v. 10) leads to Jesse, David’s father, and the line of Caleb leads to Bezalel, supervisor of the tabernacle construction in the days of Moses (Ex. 31:1–5; 35:30–36:7). The proximity of the royal family (2:10–17) to the family of Bezalel reflects the association of the throne of David with temple worship following the exile (6:1 note).
The only place where the Bible gives genealogical information about the family of Jerahmeel, who lived in southern Judah (1 Sam. 27:10; 30:27–29).

This additional information about the family of Jerahmeel concentrates on the line from Sheshan (v. 31) to Elishama (v. 41). It is possible that Elishama was a contemporary of David (the twenty-third generation of Judah), but he may have been the scribe of King Jehoiakim (Jer. 36:12, 20).

When the word “father” is associated with the name of a town or village, it probably means “founder” or “head” (1:5 note). The inclusion of settlements lying outside the control of the community would have encouraged readers of the time to consider regaining all the territories once occupied by the people of God (2:3–9:1 note).
Foreigners related by marriage to Moses and adopted by Judah (Judg. 1:16; 4:11). They are included as legitimate members of the people of God.

This material on the line of Ram, David’s ancestor (2:3–4:23 note), shows that Zerubbabel (3:19) was the legitimate heir of the Davidic line. The record of David’s family covers his children born in Hebron and Jerusalem (3:1–9); Solomon’s descendants (3:10–16); and the descendants of Jehoiachin (3:17–24). The list of these sons is from 2 Sam. 3:2–5; 5:13–16; 13:1.

David’s other sons are passed over to focus on Solomon, the chosen descendant. The royal line moves unchallenged from David to Solomon (23:1 note). Azariah (3:12) is the same person later called Uzziah (2 Chr. 26:1 note). No mention is made of Athaliah the usurper (2 Chr. 22:10–23:21).

Josiah’s firstborn, Johanan (otherwise unknown), did not succeed him. Shallum (Jehoahaz) followed Josiah (2 Kin. 23:30, 31; 2 Chr. 36:1, 2). Pharaoh Neco removed Shallum from power and replaced him with his brother Eliakim (Jehoiakim, 2 Kin. 23:32–34; 2 Chr. 36:3, 4). Jehoiakim was succeeded by his son Jehoiachin (2 Kin. 24:8–16; 2 Chr. 36:9, 10), but Nebuchadnezzar replaced Jehoiachin with Josiah’s third son, Zedekiah (2 Kin. 24:18–20; 2 Chr. 36:10–14).

Also called Jehoiachin or Coniah. The prophet Jeremiah, whose life and words were known to the writer (2 Chr. 35:25; 36:12, 21, 22), announced that God would remove Jeconiah’s family from the throne (Jer. 22:30 note). In His mercy, however, God withdrew this curse and established Jeconiah’s line once again. Jeconiah was released from prison in Babylon (2 Kin. 25:27–30). Sheshbazzar (spelled Shenazzar in 1 Chr. 3:18) brought temple treasures back to Judah (Ezra 1:11; 5:14–16). Zerubbabel (1 Chr. 3:19) was governor over the restored community after the exile in Babylon and rebuilt the temple (Ezra 3:1–13). God declared Zerubbabel His “signet ring” (Hag. 2:23), reversing the curse on Jeconiah (Jer. 22:24). Zerubbabel never became king, but his line represented the royal hopes of the community. Both Matthew (Matt. 1:12, 13) and Luke (Luke 3:27) identify Jesus, the supreme king, with this lineage.

Elsewhere (Ezra 3:2, 8; Neh. 12:1; Hag. 1:12, 14; 2:2, 23; Matt. 1:12; Luke 3:27), Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel (3:17). This may mean that Zerubbabel succeeded Pedaiah. Alternatively, Pedaiah may have become the head of the family at Shealtiel’s death, adopting Zerubbabel as his own.

Probably not descendants of Zerubbabel but other Davidic families contemporary with Zerubbabel (see text note “sons of”). If this is correct, the genealogy goes only two generations beyond Zerubbabel (Introduction: Date and Occasion). On the other hand, treating the genealogy as descending would yield six generations after Zerubbabel (eight after Jehoiakim), bringing the line down to c. 400 B.C.

The verse mentions only five. One name may have been lost as the text was copied later. It is also possible that “six” includes Shemaiah with the five sons as the descendants of Shecaniah. The line Shecaniah, Shemaiah, Neaniah, Elioenai, and Anani would extend to c. 425 B.C.

In this section, personal and clan names are mixed with place names, some of them outside the boundaries of the territory of the returned exiles (2:42 note).

**4:1 Carmi.** Probably refers to Caleb (2:7). If so, the verse gives a linear genealogy from Judah to Shobal (2:4, 5, 9, 50).

A brief example of extraordinary piety in the line of Judah. Blessing through prayer and trust in God is a major theme in Chronicles (5:18–22; 17:16–27; 21:1–22:1; 2 Chr. 6:12–42; 7:12–16; 13:14–16; 14:11–13; 18:31; 20:5–30; 30:18–20; 32:20–24; 33:11–13). In line with the geographical references in this chapter, the focus is on territorial expansion (1:5 note), victory, and safety through prayer (2 Chr. 6:34 note).
Israel’s first judge (Josh. 15:17; Judg. 1:13; 3:9–11).
Mered’s marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter is otherwise not recorded. It suggests a time when Israelites were prominent in Egypt, possibly during the days of Joseph.

Judah’s oldest surviving son (2:3). The record of Shelah includes personal names, place names, and trade guilds (linen workers, potters, and royal servants; see 1:5 note). 4:24–5:26 A number of less significant tribes are brought together in this section, which balances a similar collection of tribes in 7:1–40.

The tribe of Simeon was closely associated with the tribe of Judah (Josh. 19:1–9; Judg. 1:3). This material is of several types: genealogies (4:24–27, 34–38), geography (4:28–33), and historical notes on territorial expansion (4:39–43). For other genealogical records of the tribe of Simeon, see Gen. 46:10; Ex. 6:15; Num. 26:12–14.

This list of settlements in Simeon is drawn from Josh. 19:2–8 (see Josh. 15:26–32, where several of these villages are given to Judah). Knowing the territories held before the Babylonian exile would instill hope within the returnees for geographical expansion (2:3–9:1 note).

The writer lists some prominent leaders from Simeon (4:34–38) and then describes how they expanded their territories in several directions (4:39–43). Neh. 11:26–29 indicates that some of these cities (Moladah, Hazarshual, Beersheba, Ziklag, and En-rimmon) were resettled after the Babylonian exile. The point was to tell the readers how far the Promised Land extended.

Also v. 43. The expression “today” or “this day” in Chronicles can refer to the writer’s own time (5:26; 2 Chr. 20:26; 35:25) or to the earlier days of the sources being quoted. At times, it can even indicate the times of the sources used by the Chronicler’s sources (13:11; 2 Chr. 5:9; 8:8; 10:19; 21:10). Sometimes the expression is an idiom for “from then on” or “in perpetuity.”

The tribes east of the Jordan River are discussed. This material is in four sections: Reuben (vv. 1–10); Gad (vv. 11–17); a brief narrative (vv. 18–22); and the half-tribe of Manasseh (vv. 23–26). The hope is that these tribes will be included in the nation after the return from exile in Babylon (2:42 note).

**5:1 he was the firstborn.** The writer explains why Reuben the firstborn is given so little prominence among the tribes. He defiled his father’s bed (Gen. 35:22; 49:4) and lost his right as firstborn to the double portion of the inheritance (Deut. 21:15–17). Instead, Joseph received Reuben’s double portion through his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, who were treated as separate tribes (Gen. 48:1–22).
The ruler mentioned here is David, and by implication Zerubbabel, his descendant (11:2; 17:7; see also 2 Sam. 5:2; 6:21).

A king of Assyria (745–727 B.C.), also called Pul (v. 26). He invaded the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kin. 15:29) and also required Ahaz of Judah to pay tribute (2 Chr. 28:21 note). See the introductions to Amos, Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah.
This geographical information comes from Num. 32:37, 38, and Josh. 13:15–23.

verse_quote: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
note: This brief narrative concerns all three tribes from east of the Jordan River (cf. Num. 32). The story illustrates the importance of prayer and reliance on God in battle, a theme appearing frequently in this history (2 Chr. 6:34 note).
The Israelites overcame an army much larger than their own (v. 18; 19:7 and note).
This remark refers to the deportation of the tribes east of the Jordan River by the Assyrians in 734 B.C. (vv. 6, 26).

The tribes east of the Jordan River suffered exile because the infidelity of the half-tribe of Manasseh invited divine retribution. These events stand in contrast to the preceding narrative of prayer and blessing (vv. 18–22; see 4:9, 10).
See note on 2 Chr. 21:11.
to this day. See note on 4:41.

A lengthy account of the tribe of Levi is placed significantly at the center of the genealogies and provides the background for the arrangement of the temple personnel in the restored community following the exile in Babylon. The writer connects the Davidic monarchy with temple worship in his conception of a restored people. The discussion covers people and territories (1:5; 2:3–9:1 note). The attention given to Levi reveals the importance of the temple and priesthood. If the returning exiles were to see God’s blessing, then both the royal family (Judah) and the temple personnel (Levi) had to carry out their proper functions (29:22 note). The material covers the priests descended from Aaron, a survey of three clans of Levi, the temple musicians appointed by David (6:31–47), and the duties of the sons of Aaron and other families. This account provides a rationale for ordering the tribe of Levi in the period after the exile in Babylon.
See note on 15:11.

An interest in Solomon’s temple arrangement as a model for the community returning from the exile explains the relevance of a comment on Azariah (1 Kin. 4:2 and Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The high-priestly line is traced to Jehozadak, father of Jeshua (usually spelled Joshua), who was high priest in the early period after the exile to Babylon (Ezra 3:2; 5:2; 10:18; Hag. 1:1; 2:2; Zech. 3:1; 6:11)., 15
Probably another name for Izhar (vv. 2, 37, 38; Ex. 6:18, 21).
These men were all sons of Korah (see v. 37; Ex. 6:24)., 23
Probably alternative names for Zuph, Toah, and Eliel (vv. 34, 35)., 27
1 Sam. 1:1 traces Elkanah and his ancestors back to Zophia (Zuph) as Ephraimites. This designation may have indicated the location of his home, not his tribe (1 Sam. 1:1 note)., 28

David appointed groups from each of the three clans of Levi as musicians (15:16–26; 2 Chr. 35:3): the family of Heman from Kohath (vv. 33–38), the family of Asaph from Gershon (vv. 39–43), and the family of Ethan from Merari (vv. 44–47). The importance of music in worship is stressed (15:16 note), and what is said also gives a basis for the functions of these clans in the period following the exile in Babylon.

At the center of the Levitical genealogies are those of the all-important priestly families.

**6:49 all that Moses ... had commanded.** See note on 16:40.

Discussion of the Levitical families concludes with the exclusive right of the Zadokites to offer sacrifices because of their direct descent from Aaron. There may have been some controversy about this among the Levitical families at the time of writing (15:11 note).
Areas of countryside used for grazing.

In this account (vv. 54–81), drawing from Josh. 21:4–48, the writer points to the wide area that had belonged to Levi. Most of the places named were outside the boundaries of the province occupied following the return from exile, suggesting a hope that the restored community would expand (2:42 note).

The remaining peripheral tribes are brought together here, balancing those mentioned in 4:24–5:26.

**7:1 Issachar.** The record of Issachar is drawn from Gen. 46:13; Num. 1:28; 26:23–25. Some portions of the material stem from military lists (vv. 2, 4, 5). For the numbers of fighting men, see note on 12:23.
The writer will return to the tribe of Benjamin again in ch. 8 to trace the lineage of Saul. Here he draws upon military lists (vv. 7, 9, 11). For the numbers of fighting men see note on 12:23.
This list repeats information found in Gen. 46:24 and Num. 26:48–50.
See note on 5:23–26. Much of this data is taken from Num. 26:29–34 and Josh. 17:1–13. The focus on women in this line may stem from the importance of Zelophehad’s daughters in Num. 26:33.
Matters of lineage and geography appear again (2:3–9:1 note).
The genealogy of Asher is drawn from Gen. 46:17 and Num. 26:44–46. For the numbers of fighting men, see note on 12:23.

The survey of the tribes of Israel concludes with a second, more extensive treatment of Benjamin (see 7:6–12). The genealogy of Benjamin is comparable in length to the treatment of Judah (2:3–4:23) and Levi (6:1–81). The tribe of Benjamin is of special importance because of its close association with Judah in the days before and after the Babylonian exile (9:4–9; 1 Kin. 12:20, 21). Saul, the first king of Israel, was from the tribe of Benjamin (9:35–44; 1 Sam. 9:1–10:27). This chapter is arranged according to geography: Geba (vv. 1–7), Moab (vv. 8–13), Jerusalem (vv. 14–28), and Gibeon (vv. 29–40).

**8:1–7** Cf. the various lists in 7:6–12; Gen. 46:21; Num. 26:38–41.
For Israelites living in Moab (v. 8), see 1 Sam. 22:3–5 and Ruth 1:1, 2.
Much of this list is repeated in 9:35–44. It traces the Benjaminites in Gibeon to Saul (8:33) and many generations after him.

This is probably his original name, meaning “man of Baal,” from a time when “baal,” lord or master, could be an epithet of the one true God. Later, scribes changed the name to Ishbosheth, “man of shame” (2 Sam. 2:8). Possibly he is to be identified with Ishvi (1 Sam. 14:49).

This name for Mephibosheth was probably first spelled Meri-baal (“hero of Baal” or “loved of Baal,” see 8:33 note) and later changed to Merib-baal (perhaps “opponent of Baal”). “Mephibosheth” itself means “from the mouth of shame” (2 Sam. 4:4; 9:6).

Contains a selective summary of Israelites who made up the early community of those returning from exile in Babylon. Much of this material also appears in Neh. 11.

**9:1 all Israel.** The lists of the tribes of Israel represent the entire nation. The historical people of God and their territories are presented as a model for the community of those returning from exile in Babylon (11:1; 2 Chr. 10:1; 29:24 and notes).

The account emphasizes that the returnees took possession of land that was rightfully theirs.

**Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.** The lists that follow (vv. 4–34) cover each of these categories except the temple servants, who may have been descendants of the Gibeonites (Josh. 9:23) pressed into the mundane work required for maintaining the tabernacle (Ezra 8:20).

The Chronicler views the northern and southern kingdoms as essentially reunited under Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:1 note). Representatives of the entire nation went into the Babylonian exile and returned to the land. For this reason, the writer does not overlook Ephraim and Manasseh among those returning. Yet Judah and Benjamin are given special attention because they represent the southern kingdom, the home of the line of David and the location of the temple.
Those belonging to the tribe of Judah are traced to Judah’s sons: Perez (v. 4), Shelah (v. 5; “Shilonites” probably refers to “Shelanites”; see 2:3; 4:21–23; Num. 26:20), and Zerah (v. 6).

Levites in charge of music (6:39; 9:33; 16:41, 42). Their prominence in this list reflects the importance of music in worship (15:16 note)., 33

**9:16 Netophathites.** Netophah was a town about three miles (5 km) south of Bethlehem (Neh. 7:26; 12:28).

There is a list of gatekeepers in 26:1–19. This list reaches to the time of David (vv. 23, 24). The cycles of duty of the gatekeepers is described, evidently as a model for the new generation. David’s tabernacle required twenty-four guards. Assignments and rotations were made by lot (26:12–18).

The Levites performed a variety of functions in the temple. Special exemption was made for the musicians (15:16 note).

**1 Chr. 9:35–2 Chr. 9:31** The writer has now established the identity, order, and territory of the people of God by lists and genealogies. His next task, occupying many chapters, is to give a portrait of the united monarchy so that it may function as a pattern for the returned exiles to emulate as they engaged in restoring their community in their day. Unlike the books of Samuel, which record Saul’s rise and fall at length, Chronicles simply reports Saul’s genealogy (1 Chr. 9:35–44) and the transfer of power from Saul to David (10:1–14) before turning to the history of David (chs. 11–29) and Solomon (2 Chr. 1–9). Saul’s sin and failure, which were followed by abandonment of the land and its occupation by others (1 Chr. 10:7) provides a paradigm for the later exile. Likewise, the subsequent glories under David and Solomon provide a hope-filled paradigm for the returned exiles.

**9:35–44** The genealogy of Saul is almost identical to 8:29–40 and is repeated as a lead-in to the narrative of Saul’s death, followed by David’s accession.

The Chronicler includes the narrative of Saul’s death because of his sin (v. 13), since it enhances David’s status as appointed by God to succeed him (v. 14).

**10:1 fell slain.** The soldiers (v. 1), Saul (vv. 4, 6–8, 12–14), his sons (vv. 2, 6–8, 12), and his armor-bearer (v. 5) all die, indicating that Saul is under severe divine judgment (v. 13). The writer follows 1 Sam. 31 in his report of Saul’s suicide, defilement, and burial. He adds vv. 13, 14 to give the reason for these tragic events.

Saul’s three sons (v. 2) and his chief officers die, but Ish-bosheth (also called Eshbaal) survives (8:33; 9:39; 2 Sam. 2:8). Saul’s ruling house has come to an abrupt end, unlike David’s house (dynasty), which God establishes permanently over Israel (17:1–15 note).
See the parallel with David and Goliath (1 Sam. 17:54). The treatment of Saul’s body by his enemies highlights the dishonor of his defeat and death.

See note on 2:7. In 10:1–12, Saul’s demise is presented as the result of divine judgment. Saul dies because he has been unfaithful to the LORD by failing to “keep the command” and to “seek guidance” from God. Saul’s consultation with the medium at En-dor (strictly forbidden in Deut. 18:9–14) was the climax of his failures (1 Sam. 28).

See note on 2 Chr. 7:14.

**the LORD put him to death.** Although Saul commits suicide, his action is subject to divine control.

The reign of David is central to the history of this period. Chronicles acknowledges that David had faults (13:7–11; 21:1–7) but does not record the major failures and troubles recorded in Samuel (2 Sam. 11:1–21:14). The Chronicler is interested in establishing the lessons to be learned from David’s strengths, not his failures. The account of David’s reign focuses on two major concerns: David’s great popularity (chs. 11, 12) and his preparations for the temple (chs. 13–29). The account is arranged primarily by topic rather than chronology. The enthusiastic support for David from all over Israel should be an encouragement and model for the returned exiles, who are the original audience of the Chronicler’s work.

**11:1–12:40** Many details of the way David gained control over the land go unmentioned. These were already known to the Chronicler’s original audience from the books of Samuel. What the Chronicler does emphasize is that David did not achieve control on his own but with the wholehearted support of the people and with the assistance of special helpers.

**11:1 all Israel.** This and similar expressions are used in the narrative about the united monarchy to refer to the nation as a whole under the rule of David and Solomon and to show the Chronicler’s original audience the ideal of one nation united under one king (11:10; 12:38; 14:8; 15:3, 28; 18:14; 19:17; 21:5; 28:4, 8; 2 Chr. 1:2; 7:8; 9:30). Although the returnees to whom this work was first addressed initially had hope for an inclusive, unified kingdom under a new Davidic king, the audience’s hope was not realized until the coming of Christ, the Son of David and messianic king (2 Chr. 10:1 note; 2 Chr. 29:24 note; see also Introduction: Christ in 1 Chronicles).

verse_quote: the LORD your God said to you.
note: On several occasions in this section, it is explained that the popular support David receives is the result of God’s sovereign decree (11:3, 9, 10; 12:18, 23). A legitimate king of Israel has to be chosen by God, not merely by popular sentiment (Deut. 17:14, 15). David meets this qualification (2 Chr. 6:6).
David enters into a solemn, formal agreement with the elders, probably pledging to abide by the requirements of Deut. 17:14–20.

David’s success is demonstrated by reporting the conquest and fortification of his capital city. Successful building projects often display the blessing of God on a king. See notes on 2 Chr. 2:1–8:16; 11:5–12; 14:6, 7; 17:12; 26:9; 27:3, 4; 32:27–29.
The term means “filling” and probably refers to infilling the area between the hills of Jebus (v. 5) and Zion by means of terraced retaining walls to make the city level.

On the whole, this list of chiefs and mighty men is derived from 2 Sam. 23:8–39. The purpose is stated in the opening verse: these leaders support David’s kingship with “all Israel ... according to the word of the LORD.” The mighty acts of David’s men highlight their outstanding qualities, placing David himself in a duly favorable light.

**11:10 all Israel.** Emphasizes the strength that comes from harmony. See note on 11:1.

David’s mighty men display skill and courage by fetching water for him from behind enemy lines. In response, David shows humility by offering the water as a drink offering to the LORD (Gen. 35:14; 2 Kin. 16:13; Jer. 7:18).
The Chronicler adds to the list of David’s supporters recorded in 2 Sam. 23:39. Repeated references to tribes and locations illustrate the diverse and widespread support David enjoys.

The Chronicler assumes his audience is aware of David’s stay there as related in 1 Sam. 27. This material is out of chronological order and relates to the period before David became king.

**helped.** This term is repeated in vv. 17, 18, 19, 21, 22. David’s success depends on the effective support of others. The message to the community of the Chronicler’s day is that similar cooperation will strengthen the nation of returned exiles in Judah.
Their presence shows David as being able to attract support from those formerly hostile to him, a significant lesson for the Chronicler’s community.

At David’s wilderness stronghold (see 1 Sam. 22:14, 29; 24:1), Israelites from various locations join him. There are supporters from Gad, Benjamin, Judah, and Manasseh. See note on 11:10–47.

**12:8 faces of lions ... swift as gazelles.** Animal metaphors are common for warriors and leaders, and the men from Gad are swift and fierce.

In March and April, northern melting snows frequently swell the rivers of Palestine, making the Jordan River particularly treacherous to cross. This detail emphasizes the superior courage of David’s supporters from Gad.

By mentioning the Holy Spirit, the writer explains that the defection of men from Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, to David is not misguided. The Spirit of God directs David’s supporters.

**clothed.** See Judg. 6:34; 2 Chr. 24:20. It seems that the Spirit is compared to a garment that clothes Amasai, possibly with the result that all can detect His inspired empowerment.
While significantly abbreviating the account of 1 Sam. 29, the writer is clear that David does not fight against his fellow Israelites.
David receives further support at Ziklag (12:8–19 note).
The writer gives high praise to David’s army by comparing it to the innumerable heavenly army.

During the early part of his reign at Hebron, other supporters join David, with representatives coming from each tribe. The numbers appear very high. Several explanations of these large numbers are possible. The Hebrew word translated “thousand” may be a technical term referring to a military unit of considerably smaller size. In that case, v. 24 would read “men of Judah, carrying shield and spear, six units with (totaling) eight hundred armed for war.” Alternatively, the Hebrew consonants translated “thousand” can also be read with other vowels to mean “chiefs.” Thus, v. 24 would read “six chiefs with eight hundred armed for war.” Finally, the numbers could be figurative in nature in order to praise David’s forces (12:22 note). See Introduction: Special Issues for more on issues related to numbers in the Chronicler’s work.
Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. By grouping these tribes together and treating them as a unit, the Chronicler preserves twelve as the number of the tribes.

The report of David’s widespread support closes with the observation that the people at Hebron, and the rest of the nation, are of “a single mind” in their support of David. They celebrate their new king with joy and feasting. This happy event would have been a model for the community returning from exile in Babylon. It also prefigures the messianic banquet when Christ returns (Matt. 8:11; 22:1–10; Rev. 19:7–9).

**12:38 all Israel.** See note on 11:1.

David displays his loyalty to the LORD and his desire to promote true worship by arranging for the ark to be brought to Jerusalem. Comparison with 2 Sam. 5 and 6 indicates that the materials in Samuel and Chronicles are arranged topically and not in strict chronological order. The Chronicles account is in three parts: the initial failure to transfer the ark to Jerusalem (ch. 13); David’s blessings (ch. 14); and the successful recovery of the ark (chs. 15,16).

**13:1–4** This introduction does not appear in 2 Sam. 5 and 6. It focuses on the support of “all the assembly” for worship centralized at David’s new capital, Jerusalem (13:4–8; 11:1 note).

verse_quote: good to you ... from the LORD.
note:
The harmony between David and the people as they seek to obey God is a model for the returned exiles (2 Chr. 30:4, 5).

**brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel.** This reflects the fatalities caused by the Philistine wars.

The Chronicler contrasts David and Saul (11:2). David is concerned for the ark, while Saul neglected it. However, 1 Sam. 14:18 may favor the rendering “seek him” (see text note). Since the ark is the footstool of God’s throne, to seek the ark is to seek the LORD.

The Chronicler continues to emphasize unity as the correct basis for the action of Israel gathered from the Nile (lit. “Shihor,” perhaps the easternmost distributary of the Nile, although some identify it with the more northerly Brook of Egypt) to Lebo-hamath in the north.

**Kiriath-jearim.** About ten miles (16 km) west of Jerusalem.

**13:6 called by the name of the LORD.** A formula that denotes divine possession. The treatment accorded the ark has to be in accordance with the requirements of its divine owner, who is also pleased to occupy His property.

**who sits enthroned above the cherubim.** The ark of the covenant is the visible sign of the presence of the LORD, who condescends to dwell in the midst of His people. The cherubim function as the throne attendants of the heavenly king.

The Israelites do not observe the law of God about transporting the ark with poles on the priests’ shoulders (Ex. 25:12–15). Instead, they handle it with what they themselves consider appropriate respect (in fact, in Philistine fashion, on a cart; 1 Sam. 6:7–11), and so disregard the holiness of God and the divine regulation of worship (15:2, 11–15).
See note on 15:16.

Uzzah demonstrates a disregard for the sanctity of worship by touching the ark (Num. 4:15). Although seemingly a minor offense, Uzzah’s violation involves carelessness for the holiness of God, which calls for judgment that would be a warning to all (v. 7 note).
See note on 4:41.

David’s initial reaction of anger (v. 11), because his plans had been upset, is replaced with fear as the reminder of the holiness of God brought home to him the awesome nature of the project in which he is engaged.

He is an appropriate caretaker for the ark since he is a Levite (15:18, 21, 24) from the region of Gath. He is blessed with many sons (26:4, 5) presumably because he cares properly for the ark. Chronicles often mentions numerous children as a sign of divine approval and blessing (14:3; 2 Chr. 11:18–23; 13:21).

The account of David’s blessings is gathered from various sources and placed between David’s two attempts to relocate the ark. This illustrates that despite David’s initial failure (ch. 13), God establishes and blesses him because of his

**heart commitment.** Three items appear: palace preparations (14:1, 2), David’s children in Jerusalem (vv. 3–7), and David’s victory over the Philistines (vv. 8–17).

**14:1 Hiram.** David seems to have entered into a treaty relationship with Hiram, king of the Phoenicians. As well as being renowned as seamen, they are highly skilled craftsmen who have ready access to suitable building timber from Lebanon.

verse_quote: the LORD had established ... exalted for the sake of his people.
note: David recognizes that the establishment of his kingdom is a blessing for the people. After their exile in Babylon, the original readers would have been encouraged by these remarks in their hope for a new Davidic king (2 Chr. 2:11 note).

As well as a palace, David acquires a harem, a practice commonly accepted among the oriental kings of his day. Deuteronomy 17:17, however, warns the kings of Israel not to take many wives. David’s willingness to take on additional wives eventually leads to the greatest crisis of his reign and violence in his own household (2 Sam. 11:1–12:15). While polygamy is regulated in Scripture, this is a concession to fallen humanity and not the ideal or original intent for mankind. Those who practice it experience discord in their families and, in Solomon’s case, spiritual waywardness (cf. Gen. 16; 21:1–21; 30:1–24; 1 Kings 11:1–8). Jesus tells us that God designed marriage to be a union of one man and one woman (Matt. 19:3–9).

David’s victory over the Philistines contrasts with Saul’s defeat (10:1–7). David inquires of the LORD (14:10, 14), while Saul consulted a medium (10:13). This victory also contrasts with David’s failed attempt to retrieve the ark (13:1–14). While David was angered because the LORD had “broken out” against Uzzah (13:11), he now declares that “God has broken through” against the Philistines (14:11).

**14:8 all Israel.** See note on 11:1.
Possibly three miles (5 km) southwest of Jerusalem.

David follows Mosaic regulations in these actions (Deut. 7:5, 25). The burning is not mentioned in 2 Sam. 5:21, but there is evidence that the Chronicler is reproducing other source material available to him.

A distance of about fifteen miles (25 km). Gibeon is six miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem, and Gezer, which is under Philistine control at this time, is situated in the foothills on the edge of the coastal plain, twenty miles (31 km) west of Jerusalem.

verse_quote: fear of him upon all nations.
note: This verse is in addition to the account of 2 Sam. 5, highlighting David’s international fame (v. 1 note). David stands strong against his enemies. Other nations see the power of God in the king’s victory and fear (Josh. 2:11; 2 Chr. 17:10; 20:29). Readers of the book are encouraged to hope for a new David who will overthrow secular worldly powers (Hag. 2:6, 7, 20–23; Zech. 9:1–13).

This account of the ark’s recovery provides the background for David’s involvement in organizing the Levites and the worship that will take place in Jerusalem. Eight verses (15:25–16:3) parallel 2 Sam. 6:12–19.

**15:1 pitched a tent.** The tabernacle is still in Gibeon (16:39). It is not known why David chooses to construct a new tent to shelter the ark rather than move the tabernacle.
This verse and vv. 13–15 show that David transfers the ark in compliance with Mosaic law (Ex. 25:12–15; Deut. 10:8; 18:5).

All three divisions of the tribe of Levi (Kohathites, Merarites, and Gershonites) are included in David’s worship organization, providing a model for Levitical orders after the nation’s exile in Babylon (6:1–53 and notes).

The two high priests during David’s reign. Zadok serves at the tabernacle in Gibeon (16:39), and Abiathar serves in Jerusalem (18:16; 27:34 and notes). Solomon later excludes Abiathar because of his support of Adonijah’s bid for the throne (1 Kin. 1:7; 2:26, 27). This leaves Zadok and his descendants as the highpriestly family in Jerusalem (6:1, 53 and notes).
See note on 16:40.

An interest in the music of worship is apparent in Chronicles; see 1 Chr. 6:31–47; 9:15, 16, 33; 13:8; 15:28; 16:4–6; 23:5; 25:1–7; 2 Chr. 5:12, 13; 7:6; 23:13; 29:25–30; 34:12. This is a new aspect of the ministry of the Levites, introduced in preparation for temple worship. This emphasis is doubtless related to a concern for the restoration of proper worship in the period following the return from exile in Babylon (6:1–81 note).
The robe of fine linen and the linen ephod are the usual clothing of priests (1 Sam. 2:18; 22:18).
See note on 11:1.

Attention is drawn to the hardened heart of Saul’s daughter. In contrast to the people, the Levites, and David, Michal is disgusted by the enthusiastic worship. Michal’s sarcastic rebuke (2 Sam. 6:20) is not repeated here, perhaps to avoid casting doubt on the purity of David’s worship.
The Davidic arrangement of the Levites is noted (6:1–81 note).
See note on 15:16.

A psalm of celebration not found in Samuel. The passage is similar to portions of several psalms (cf. vv. 8–22 with Ps. 105:1–15; vv. 23–33 with Ps. 96; vv. 34–36 with Ps. 106:1, 47, 48). David celebrates the entry of the ark into Jerusalem as a mighty act of God, and his words have continuing value for those returning to Jerusalem from the exile in Babylon. David calls for the praise of God (vv. 8–13). He remembers the promise of the land and the protection of God in the wanderings of the past (vv. 15–22). Later readers experience similar blessings in their return to the land. David invites the people to cry out for further protection and deliverance (v. 35). Those returned from Babylon need the same help from God. Finally, the people respond with praise and joy at the blessings of God (v. 36), just as later readers should praise God in their day.
See note on 2 Chr. 7:14.

The text of this verse has been somewhat corrupted (see text note and Introduction: Special Issues). It is unclear how many Levites have the name Obed-edom. One suggestion is that there are two: a musician (15:21; 16:5), who may also look after the ark (13:13), and a gatekeeper (15:18, 24; 26:4, 8, 15). Alternatively, only one man may be involved, and his varied designation may reflect changes over the long years of David’s reign.
minister at Gibeon where the tabernacle and the altar of burnt offering are still situated at this time, presumably awaiting the building of the temple.

verse_quote: all that is written in the Law of the LORD.
note: David’s commitment to observing Mosaic law is presented as a model for the reorganization of the community after the return from exile in Babylon (6:49; 15:15; 22:12, 13; 2 Chr. 6:16; 12:1, 2; 14:4; 17:3–9; 24:6, 9; 25:4; 30:15, 16; 31:3–21; 33:8; 34:19–33; 35:6–26). See Introduction: Characteristics and Themes.

David makes a most important contribution to Israel’s history by preparing for the temple. This account has six major sections: David’s being commissioned by God (ch. 17); making military preparations (chs. 18–20); discovering the temple site (21:1–22:1); commissioning builders (22:2–19); arranging personnel (chs. 23–27); and leading national celebration and exhortation (chs. 28; 29).

**17:1–27** David’s commission from God to prepare for the temple is in two parts: Nathan’s dynastic oracle (17:1–15) and David’s prayer of acceptance (17:16–27). The writer follows 2 Sam. 7 closely. In neither passage is the term “covenant” used of this divine disclosure, but other Scriptures warrant the use of the designation “Davidic covenant” (e.g. 2 Sam 23:5; Ps. 89:3).

**17:1–15 The word “house” lies at the heart of this passage.** David sees his own house (“palace”) and desires to build a “house” (a temple) for God. But God declares that He will build a “house” (a dynasty; v. 10) for David. David’s son will build a “house” (a temple; v. 12) for the LORD. The Davidic covenant inaugurates the dynasty and the temple as the two covenant institutions that ground the identity of Israel as God’s covenant servants and as recipients of His blessing, particularly that of His presence in their midst. Both of these roles are realized in Christ (Rom. 1:3; John 2:21). The Chronicler’s focus is on how Solomon fulfills the terms of the covenant. In this respect, Solomon is a type of Christ, anticipating what He will bring to consummation.

**17:1, 10** The Chronicler does not repeat the references to David’s rest from enemies, found in 2 Sam. 7:1, 11. The emphasis is that David is a man of war (but see 17:8; 22:18) and therefore unqualified to build the temple (22:6–10 note)., 10
Nathan’s reply is based on how he interprets God’s providential dealings with David, but since David has consulted him as a prophet, Nathan ought to have inquired of the LORD before replying.

verse_quote: the word of the LORD came.
note: Nathan is now in a position to deliver an authoritative, truly prophetic response.

Nathan announces the dynastic promises associated with the Davidic covenant. The covenant with David is also celebrated in Pss. 89 and 132. The LORD promises that David’s descendants will become a dynasty, ruling always over Israel. Individual kings might become subject to severe chastisement (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 89:30–32), but the line of David will never be permanently rejected from the throne (2 Sam. 7:15, 16; 2 Chr. 6:16; Pss. 89:33–37; 132:11, 12). This covenant is a basis for hope that Israel can be fully restored (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The NT reveals that the promises to David are fulfilled in Christ. Christ has kept the conditions of the covenant perfectly (Heb. 4:15); He serves as the mediator of the covenant of grace (Acts 2:25–36; Heb. 9:15); and He promises to return as conquering king (Matt. 24:29–31; Mark 13:24–27; Luke 21:25–28).

verse_quote: to him a father ... to me a son.
note:
This language indicates a special adoption of the chosen king, not a belief in the divinity of the king as in other ancient Near Eastern cultures (Pss. 2:7; 45:6; 89:27 and note). NT writers understand these words about Solomon as a foreshadowing of Christ, the final Davidic king (Mark 1:11; Luke 1:32, 33; Heb. 1:5). Christ is the Son of David, but He is also the Son of God. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35) and is the second person of the Godhead (John 1:1–18; 17:1).

The Chronicler does not mention the imposition of divine discipline when David’s son goes astray (2 Sam. 7:14b), presumably because this would detract from his portrayal of Solomon as a role model.

“My” twice replaces “your” in 2 Sam. 7:16 to bring out the fundamental perspective of the Chronicler that the LORD is the only source of power and authority in Israel (see 28:5; 2 Chr. 1:11; 9:8; 13:8).

**his throne shall be established forever.** God designates David’s line as the permanent dynasty over His people. When David’s descendants fail, they are chastised (2 Sam. 7:14), but God always raises up another son of David to continue the line. This promise gave hope to the postexilic community, and it comes to fulfillment in Jesus, who reigns on the throne of David forever (vv. 7–14 note; 2 Chr. 21:7).

Who am I. David’s sincere expression of humility sets an attractive and valuable example (29:14–16; 2 Chr. 2:6). He recognizes that there is an overwhelming instance of divine grace in granting and fulfilling the covenant (see John 1:16; Eph. 2:7).
The memory of all that God has revealed Himself to be; His reputation (see 2 Chr. 6:5).

This section concerns David’s military and political accomplishments. Relying on 2 Sam. 8; 10; 11; and 21, it is organized in four sections: a survey of victories (18:1–13); a list of officials (18:14–17); victory over the Ammonites (19:1–20:3); and victory over the Philistines (20:4–8). This material demonstrates how David establishes the political security necessary for temple construction in Solomon’s day (18:13 note; 22:17–19). Second, it offers the background for David’s enormous material contributions to the temple construction (18:8, 11 note). Tribute from hostile nations was a major source of finance for building the temple. Third, it anticipates David’s disqualification from temple building because of his warfare (22:6–10 note; 28:3). Fourth, David’s victories inspired the readers to hope for victory over the enemies of their day (19:1–20:3 note). David’s involvement with Mephibosheth (2 Sam. 9; 21:1–14) is omitted, as is his adultery with Bathsheba and its aftermath (2 Sam. 11–20; 10:14 note). These are not relevant to the Chronicler’s theme at this point: the fulfillment of God’s covenant promises to David (17:10; 18:13).

**18:1–13** This summary of David’s wars with the Philistines to the west (v. 1), with Moab to the east (v. 2), with the Syrians (Arameans) to the north (vv. 3–11), and with Edom to the southeast (vv. 12, 13) corresponds to 2 Sam. 8:1–14. The only noteworthy omission in the account is David’s severe treatment of the Moabites (2 Sam. 8:2).

**18:1 After this.** This marker functions as a logical transition rather than noting chronological succession from ch. 17.
A Syrian (Aramean) kingdom north of Damascus, evidently intent on expanding northward to the Euphrates.

According to the parallel text in 2 Sam. 8:4, David captured “1,700.” However, an ancient translation of 2 Samuel agrees with 1 Chronicles in reading “7,000.” It may be that the number of captives indicated in the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel that we possess was inadvertently miscopied at some point. If so, the Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles that we possess actually preserves what the author of 2 Samuel originally wrote while the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel that we possess does not. See Introduction: Special Issues.

David devotes the spoils of warfare to temple construction, preparing the way for Solomon to build.

**18:11 Edom ... Amalek.** This list of enemies covers most of the armies mentioned in chs. 18–20.

David’s nephew, son of his half sister Zeruiah, is given the credit for the victory rather than David himself (2 Sam. 8:13). Joab also contributes much to this success (1 Kin. 11:15, 16; Psalm 60 superscription). The Valley of Salt is in Edomite territory at the southern end of the Dead Sea.

verse_quote: the LORD gave victory to David.
note: David’s victories provide a secure political environment that will allow Solomon to concentrate on building (19:1–20:3 note).
David’s domestic arrangements also contribute to the political stability necessary for building projects (18:1–20:8 note). The Chronicler carries over the expression “all Israel” from 2 Sam. 8:15.

verse_quote: Zadok ... Ahimelech the son of Abiathar.
note: See note on 15:11.

Foreign mercenaries among the king’s guards (1 Sam. 30:14 note).

**chief officials.** Whereas 2 Sam. 8:18 uses the term “priests” in connection with David’s sons, the Chronicler employs a term more definitely referring to high political office. David and his sons are not technically priests, and the writer is being more precise about the proper ordering of royalty and priesthood (6:1–81 note).

Cf. 2 Sam. 10:1–19; 11:1; 12:29–31 and notes. For the omission of David’s sin with Bathsheba and the ensuing troubles in the Davidic house (2 Sam. 11:1–21:14) see note on 18:1–20:8.

**19:1 Ammonites.** The Ammonites, whose territory was east of the Jordan and north of Moab, are longstanding enemies of Israel (Judg. 10:7–9; 10:17–11:40; 1 Sam. 11:1–11; 14:47). They also trouble the community after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh. 2:19; 4:3, 7, 8).
Chronicles replaces the less familiar Beth-rehob with Mesopotamia (Aram-naharim, meaning “Aram of the two rivers,” referring to northern Mesopotamia) and omits the reference to Tob (2 Sam. 10:6).

Israel’s victory is frequently highlighted by reporting the numbers of the opposing army (2 Chr. 12:2–4; 13:3; 14:9).

**Medeba.** An old Moabite town, twelve miles (19 km) east of the Dead Sea, nominally in Reubenite territory but frequently changing hands. At this point, Medeba is under Ammonite control.
See note on 11:1.
2 Sam. 10:18 reads “700.” It is possible that the higher number in Chronicles is due to a inadvertent copying error in the transmission of the text. See Introduction: Special Issues.

Armies typically advance after the first spring harvest, when food is more abundant (2 Sam. 11:1; 1 Kin. 20:22, 26).

**Rabbah.** In David’s day, the major city of the Ammonites; now Amman, the capital of Jordan.
See note on 18:8, 11.

Brief notes are given of three Philistine wars, corresponding to 2 Sam. 21:18–22.

**20:4 after this.** See note on 18:1.

**were subdued.** Not found in 2 Sam. 21:18. The sentence indicates that the promise of 17:10 is fulfilled (2 Chr. 13:18; cf. 28:19).

The history continues with David’s discovery of the temple site (17:1–29:30 note). The theme of military victory (19:1–20:8) leads to an account of David’s census to assess the potential size of his army (v. 5). With two major exceptions, the account follows 2 Sam. 24 closely (21:1; 21:28–22:1 and notes). The author of 2 Samuel reports how David brings trouble on the nation but successfully intercedes on its behalf (2 Sam. 24). In Chronicles, the point of the story is to tell how God leads David to discover the holy site for the temple.

**21:1 Satan stood.** When the Hebrew word satan is used with a definite article, it means lit. “the adversary” (Job 1:6; Zech. 3:1). Here satan is used for the first time without a definite article, probably as a proper name (see “Satan” at Job 1:6). According to 1 Sam. 24:1, it is God who moves David. God Himself tempts no one (James 1:13), but He employs created means under His sovereign control. Chronicles identifies Satan as the instrument by which David is led astray. The two passages together remind us that God is sovereign over all events, including temptation and sin (cf. Ex. 4:21 note; Josh. 11:20; 1 Kin. 22:22, 23; 2 Chr. 10:15 note; Job 1:12; 2:10; Ezek. 3:20; 14:9; Matt. 6:13; Acts 4:27, 28).

verse_quote: a cause of guilt for Israel.
note: Taking a census is not prohibited by OT law, though there are specific regulations (Ex. 30:12; Num. 1:2; 26:2). David’s desire for a count of his military personnel may be an indication of reliance on human might rather than on divine power (2 Chr. 13:18 and note). Joab’s response (21:6; 27:24) may indicate that David has insisted that the tribe of Levi be counted for military service as well (v. 6 note).
A condensing of 2 Sam. 24:5–8.

2 Sam. 24:9 reads simply “Israel.” See note on 11:1.

**1,100,000.** Resolving the differences between these numbers from those in 2 Sam. 24:9 (“in Israel there were 800,000 ... and the men of Judah were 500,000”) is a challenge. It may be that the Chronicler is including the men from Judah in the total for “all Israel” (that is, including Judah with 470,000, not “and in Judah”). The book of Chronicles may exclude some elements, such as Levi and Benjamin, from its count (21:6 note). Or the numbers may be approximations. There might also be issues with the scribal transmission of the numbers found at this point. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

Joab does not completely carry through the census David had ordered (v. 3 note).

**Levi and Benjamin.** These tribes are not included in the census. The tribe of Levi is to be excluded from any military census, according to Mosaic law (Num. 1:49; 2:33). Benjamin may be excluded because the tabernacle is in Gibeon (v. 29).
The census of men who can be called up for military service shows that David is trusting in human strategies rather than relying in faith on the LORD.
Gad has been a wise counselor to David since the time he was a fugitive from Saul (1 Sam. 22:3–5).
“Sword” is used as a metaphor for the divine imposition of a judicial penalty.

Despite the severity of divine chastisement, David trusts in the abundant mercy of the LORD. Undoubtedly, the promises to David in 17:1–14 supply a background to David’s confident trust in God’s mercy.
The judgment involved in the pestilence appropriately weakens David’s false source of confidence.

In His mercy, the LORD spares Jerusalem from destruction.

**the angel who was working destruction.** A further reference to the angel of the LORD (see Gen. 16:7 note; 2 Sam. 24:16 note).

This verse is not found in the traditional Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Sam. 24. However, recently discovered texts of Samuel (Dead Sea Scrolls) and other witnesses suggest that the writer of Samuel probably included it in the first edition of his work. See Introduction: Special Issues.

**lifted his eyes and saw.** David is permitted to perceive spiritual reality that is ordinarily hidden from mankind. But the appearance of the angel is on this occasion visible to others (v. 20).

David reveals a shepherd’s concern for his flock under his care and pleads that any further imposition be against himself and his family and not on the people. However, Israel is not fault free, for the LORD’s anger had existed against them before the census (2 Sam. 24:1).
One of the original inhabitants of Jerusalem.

Although these verses about Ornan (spelled Araunah in 2 Sam. 24) do not appear in the traditional Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Sam. 24:20, recently discovered texts of the books of Samuel among the Dead Sea Scrolls and other witnesses suggest that the author of Samuel included these verses in the first edition of his work. This portion of the account is reminiscent of Abraham’s purchase of the burial site for Sarah (Gen. 23). David purchases the site at full price. As a result, the future temple site (21:28–22:1 note) is a royal possession devoted to the temple.

2 Sam. 24:24 reads, “the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.” It has been suggested that Samuel focuses on the threshing floor with its oxen, while Chronicles gives the value of the whole site.

verse_quote: the LORD answered him with fire.
note: This rare occurrence indicates God’s special approval of David’s actions (Lev. 9:24; 1 Kin. 18:37, 38), and prompts David’s recognition that this is to be the site of the temple. The descent of the fire anticipates Solomon’s temple dedication later at this same site (2 Chr. 7:1).

These verses are not found in 2 Sam. 24. They show an interest in sacrifice (21:28) and possibly help explain David’s neglect of the tabernacle (21:29, 30). The main point is that David recognizes the threshing floor of Ornan as the site for the future temple (22:1). This remarkable ending with its clear account of moral failure in David’s life indicates vividly the place to which the community must turn for sacrifice, forgiveness, and answered prayer (2 Chr. 3:1; 6:12–42 and notes).

This long section about David’s life is found only in Chronicles. The narrative contains David’s final preparations for constructing the temple, which begin and end with assemblies held by royal authority (22:2–19; 28:1–29:20) where similar instructions are given (cf. 22:8 with 28:3; 22:13 with 28:20; and 22:17 with 28:21). Though not yet active in his own right, Solomon begins to figure prominently alongside David. The Chronicler emphasizes that building the temple is the joint achievement of David and Solomon.

**22:2–19** David’s arrangements for constructing the temple begin with the assembling of a suitable workforce (22:2–4). David also explains to Solomon what is required of him (22:5–16) and exhorts the leaders of the land to cooperate in the enterprise (22:17–19).

**22:2 aliens.** David and Solomon use conscripted labor made up primarily of foreigners (1 Kin. 5:13–18; 9:15–23; 11:28; 2 Chr. 2:2, 17, 18; 8:7–10).

Presumably taken from the Philistines, whom David conquered (1 Sam. 13:19–22).

**bronze.** Taken from the spoils of war (18:8, 11 note).

Solomon lacks the experience to handle the responsibility of preparing for the temple (see 29:1; 2 Chr. 13:7).

**preparation.** The central theme of this section is how David provides virtually everything for the temple built by Solomon, including plans, materials, workers, work assignments, political stability, and popular support. In effect, the temple is a joint project of David and Solomon (22:2–29:20; 2 Chr. 2:3 and notes). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

David explains to Solomon why he is barred from building the temple. 1 Kin. 5:3–5 states that David has been preoccupied with warfare, and this passage specifically affirms that David has been ritually defiled by bloodshed, so he cannot be directly involved in the building (2 Chr. 6:9). This seems to be a private meeting; the public declaration will follow later (28:8). The process of transfer of leadership resembles the transfer that occurred when Joshua succeeded Moses (see Deut. 31:7, 8).

In his old age (he is about seventy), David effectively leaves the running of the country in Solomon’s hands, but not without first setting up an appropriate administrative structure. In accordance with the Chronicler’s priorities, he first presents David’s organization of religious personnel (23:2–26:32) and then of the civilian officials (ch. 27). These arrangements for Solomon’s reign also provide a model for the postexilic community.

**23:1** This opening verse is a topical heading for 23:1–29:25.

**he made Solomon his son king over Israel.** Apparently assuming his readers’ knowledge of the books of Kings, the Chronicler has said little about the checkered history of David’s rise to power or the troubles of his reign (11:1–29:30 note). Similarly, he does not discuss Solomon’s struggle for the throne (1 Kings 1; 2), presenting a smooth transition of power from David to Solomon. Apparently, the age at which Levites began service was adjusted according to need: thirty years (Num. 4:1–3), twenty-five years (Num. 8:23–25), and twenty years (1 Chr. 23:24, 27). The music of worship is mentioned many times in this chapter (15:16 note), seemingly reflecting a special interest of the Chronicler, who wants to promote it in the rebuilt temple of his own day.

**25:1 chiefs of the service.** Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun have already been assigned the role of temple musicians, which is here extended in perpetuity to their descendants. It may be that David consults Levitical leaders in the matter, but elsewhere “chiefs of the service” is rendered “commanders of the army,” whom David consults on other occasions regarding religious affairs (see 13:1; 15:25). Military involvement in the arrangements for temple music is not altogether improbable, as the Levites provide musical accompaniment for the army as it goes into battle (see 2 Chron. 13:12; 20:22).

**prophesied.** Temple personnel are seen in prophetic roles on several occasions (2 Chr. 20:14–17; 24:19–22; 29:30; 35:15; see also 2 Kin. 23:2 with 2 Chr. 34:30). The term “prophesied” may perhaps imply authoritative declaration of divine revelation accompanied by music; alternatively, it may describe a broader aspect of the Spirit’s work of empowering people for leadership. As is the case for the seventy elders of the time of Moses (Num. 11:25, 26) and for Saul (1 Sam. 10:10–12), “prophesying” does not always denote divine revelation of the kind received by the writing prophets. This theme may suggest the role of priests as guides for the restoration of the community after the return from exile in Babylon (Zech. 6:9–15).

verse_quote: If you seek him ... if you forsake him.
note: Basic covenantal conditions apply to the promises given to David and his line. Though the Davidic dynasty itself will not be rejected, individual kings and the nation may suffer severely under God’s judgment for apostasy. For similar expressions of this principle, see 2 Chr. 6:14, 16; 7:17–22; 15:2; 16:7–9; 19:2, 3; 21:12–15; 24:20; 34:23–28. See also Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

verse_quote: the plan of all that he had in mind.
note: Lit. “all which was in/by the spirit with him.” These words may refer to what was divinely revealed to him. Although David actively plans for the temple, his efforts are directed by the Holy Spirit. This underlines the need for the postexilic community to follow the patterns established for the temple by David and Solomon (see the example of Moses, Ex. 25:9, 40).

David has kept a written record of all that the LORD has revealed to him in this matter. The expression is, however, somewhat unusual and may point to a parallel with Moses (Ex. 31:18; 32:16). “From the hand of the LORD” is used in 2 Chr. 29:25 of a written prophetic record.

The language resembles Joshua’s commission (22:13 note). It also echoes what David said in his earlier speech (22:11–13). 29:29). Martin Luther referred to two aspects of God—the hidden and the revealed. A portion of the divine knowledge remains hidden to our gaze. We work in the light of what God has revealed.
